items.title: Amp puts AI agents to work beyond code with OpenAI models
items.summary: See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT-6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT-Live-1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.
items.full_text: Amp ⁠ (opens in a new window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages. Amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.” “Our users really appreciate the consistency with which OpenAI models have been getting better and better.” —Quinn Slack, CEO and member of technical staff, Amp As builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp users consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of. To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn says it gives Amp users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task. “Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he says. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to plan, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship. Amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn says. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for new users and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels. For that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards. “We have a very unique design style and writing style. We’re very picky about this, but we’ve been really happy with how GPT-6 Astra does.” —Quinn Slack, CEO and member of technical staff, Amp Quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the plans for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he says. Amp recently announced Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem. With Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, users can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run. Amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn says the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result. “People have not seen a model that’s this good, that’s this fast.” —Quinn Slack, CEO and member of technical staff, Amp For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn says.

items.title: SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours
items.summary: With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.
items.full_text: Reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover new information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, says OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours. By reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.” “Something that would’ve taken a top-flight researcher four or six weeks to do, AI is now doing at human-level output in something like eight hours.” —Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples. Stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he says. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds. Historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or important threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart says. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats. “Faster reverse engineering enables us to map a much larger part of the malware landscape and keep pace with how it changes. That gives our researchers a clearer picture of how threats are connected and how those relationships evolve.” —Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne Faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation. Comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart says, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.” Within SentinelOne, Stewart says access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate issues themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists. Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security issues as they build. “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by providing expert level cyber capability to everyone in the development team.” —Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer, SentinelOne Join the new era of work More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI.

items.title: How Third Moment Research runs 10,000 agents for 36+ hours
items.summary: With GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.
items.full_text: Every company has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success. ⁠ (opens in a new window) Third Moment Research ⁠ (opens in a new window) believes the best agents should be really good at that specific work and should improve their capabilities the more they’re used. The company is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems. The team uses those scenarios to improve agents, repeating the process as new issues emerge. Codex, GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol support the system’s research and computational work, enabling Third Moment to run 10,000 agents at once on investigations lasting 36-48 hours. The company also uses Daybreak to test the security of the environments where agents work. “In a single session, GPT-6.1 Sol is able to maintain a coherent thread of computational research across days of compute without losing the plot.” —Adam Khakhar, Co-founder, Third Moment Research One of Third Moment’s early applications is in the field of quantitative finance given the clear measure of success. This domain provides a concrete setting to study how agents work and where they struggle. The team uses Codex to find and address problems in the research environment. In one instance, it used Codex with GPT‑5.6, the latest GPT model at the time, to analyze thousands of recorded simulation trajectories (the agents’ actions and the environment’s responses) alongside timestamps and the codebase. Codex uncovered a bottleneck: backtesting a trading strategy across a year of order-level US equity data took several hours. While waiting, agents repeatedly polled for completion, wasting tokens and filling their context with status checks. After profiling the backtest and analyzing its inputs and usage, Codex identified a caching optimization and a memory-packing technique. It experimented with solutions and deployed the fix to production, reducing the backtest from approximately 3 hours to approximately 3 to 5 minutes. This reduced token use and context pollution, freeing more of the agents’ token budget for further experiments. Third Moment gives each agent the tools, information, and environment it needs for a specific job. For quantitative research, the team runs the default Codex harness inside a Dockerized environment. Agents receive a terabyte of data, documentation, and a research repository with modules for feature engineering, GPU-supported model training, trading strategies, and simulation. GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol provide the reasoning, while the Codex harness gives agents tools to act, create plans, set objectives, spawn subagents, and compact context as work continues. To address agents that stop before completing a task, Third Moment treats Codex as a subagent within an outer harness powered by GPT‑6 Sol or GPT‑6.1 Sol. The outer harness examines the trajectory when a task is left unfinished and determines whether to retry, terminate the job, or escalate to human review. “The Codex harness is extremely versatile, and it enables use across many different domains.” —Adam Khakhar, Co-founder, Third Moment Research In that research environment, agents work to improve a baseline trading system built by Third Moment’s engineers. They test trading strategies on historical data, assess whether an improvement is meaningful or noise, and use each result to choose the next experiment. According to Adam, their work has improved the baseline trading system. Before GPT‑5.5, Adam says models could only execute experiments prescribed by a user. With GPT‑5.5 and GPT‑5.6, models working with the Codex harness could use results to design follow-up experiments. Now with GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, agents can investigate root causes through hundreds of experiments running in parallel with subagents. That progression has helped agents explore research directions the team hadn’t anticipated. In one session, GPT‑6.1 Sol identified the impact of non-displayed trades on an exchange where those trades accounted for an unexpectedly large share of volume. “This was an unobvious result that our research team did not initially consider,” says Adam. Third Moment evaluates models across optimization, machine learning systems, and quantitative research. It tests frontier releases at their highest reasoning settings, assessing their ability to navigate repositories, write efficient code, and sustain an investigation. Current testing also includes GPT‑6 Luna. “GPT-6.1 Sol is currently our most-used model given its token efficiency. It completes tasks with the fewest tokens while delivering performance similar to GPT-6 Astra.” —Jeffrey Yan, Co-founder, Third Moment Research One benchmark asks agents to reduce a live scoreboard service’s update latency while preserving its outputs. The team measures speedup by dividing the average runtime of an expert-crafted solution by that of the model’s solution on the same hardware, subject to correctness. GPT‑6 Astra delivered the biggest speedup, according to Adam. For targeted work, including checks for specific security weaknesses in the simulation system, the team uses more efficient models like GPT‑5.6 Terra. For deep research, Adam believes stronger reasoning can justify higher cost: “In the space of quantitative finance, the value of finding some interesting signal is extremely high.” With 10,000 agents running autonomously, Third Moment needs a way to test the security of its research environments at scale. The team uses the Daybreak cybersecurity platform to automate that testing before simulations launch. The tests check whether an agent could break out of its research environment and access the wider network. “By using Daybreak, we’re able to have agents themselves do penetration testing on the simulation and test the infrastructure and security of it,” says Adam. “Without Daybreak, we would not be able to autonomously test this at scale.” —Adam Khakhar, Co-founder, Third Moment Research Third Moment’s ambition extends to the specialized work companies do every day. For a retailer, that could mean making better supply chain decisions when inventory is short or a supplier is delayed. For an engineering team, it could mean finding performance bottlenecks in a large codebase. For a document-heavy business, it could mean identifying where commitments in one document don’t match outcomes recorded in another. Building on the reasoning capabilities of GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Third Moment plans to expand from individual investigations to hundreds of thousands of collaborating subagents. Its roadmap calls for trillions of tokens supporting chains of dozens of dependent experiments, with the goal of using that research to autonomously improve agents as new challenges arise. For Adam, this would give people more capacity to shape how agents learn and work: “Humans can be in a much more leveraged position, where they can think about how to do research and optimize the research itself instead of actually doing the research.”

items.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
items.summary: Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI. Its security team investigates threats faster and proposes patches in minutes.
items.full_text: At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. “AI is compressing the time from human intent to action. For a while, it was assumed that there was an attacker advantage since they’re faster and more nimble. But with things like Daybreak and the advancements in OpenAI’s tooling, defenders are able to fight fire with fire and keep up with the rapid pace of AI adoption.” —James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, Block Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% boost to triage throughput. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. That would free security teams to spend less time patching and more time on preventative, strategic work. “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by putting these advanced capabilities in everyone’s hands,” he says. “It’s typically only been in very high-profile technology companies and government hands. But everyone, including critical infrastructure, schools, small businesses, can now start utilizing this technology to defend their networks.” Join the new era of work More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI.

items.title: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks
items.summary: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench, simply independently confirm their claims.
items.full_text: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench , simply independently confirm their claims. About 20,000 joined AIE NYC today for keynotes from the frontier of AI x Finance, from Anthropic showing how they are building the modern AI Financial Services stack , Vals AI CEO discussing their principles behind benchmarking models like Argon, and Coatue’s Head of AI showing how they turn news into investment decisions. All keynotes are transcribed here and all talks/workshops will be released ASAP. Tune in tomorrow for Day 3: AI News for 10/12/2026-10/13/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Frontier Model Launches: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Gemini 4 Argon : Google released Argon globally for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber defense. Access spans the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform; Google AI Pro and Ultra in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search; and Ultra in Antigravity. The official rollout supersedes an earlier newsletter claim that access was restricted to cybersecurity defenders ( announcement ). Pricing : Introductory API rates are $2/$10 per million input/output tokens , with cached input discounted 95%. Artificial Analysis reports that rates double to $4/$20 after November 30 —an important qualification for cost comparisons ( Google pricing , discount schedule ). Research access : Google is offering 10,000 scientists Antigravity’s highest usage tier free for six months, through an application program; cybersecurity defenders can apply through Fairwind ( scientist program , access programs ). Google’s internal results : Google says Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six-million-line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes. It also reports 35% more agentic code submissions , with rollbacks reduced by nearly one-third. These are internal deployment claims, not controlled productivity measurements ( engineering results ). Physical-task demonstration : DeepMind researchers describe Argon deriving a cornhole simulation from human video, performing system identification and refining throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot before achieving seven consecutive successful throws. Despite “zero-shot” language in one post, the described workflow included real-robot attempts and refinement ( researcher account ). Developer distribution : Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort , on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 ( Cursor , Devin , Copilot ). App integration : Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify ( coding interface , connected apps ). Muse Wonder’s positioning : Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case ( capability discussion , Meta positioning ). Muse rollout and economics : Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison ( pricing complaint , weekly allowance ). Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World Reliability Argon’s capability–cost position : Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index ( evaluation ). Metric interpretation : AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. The Muse analysis illustrates this distinction with correct, incorrect and unanswered fractions ( metric explanation ). Agent leaderboard : Arena places Argon High fifth, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra at Max effort. Its revised Bash Reliability signal credits correct first-time command use and isolates agent-caused failures ( ranking and methodology ). Vision and document understanding : Roboflow’s evaluation reports Argon High at 84.7% text localization/recognition versus Astra’s 76.8%, and 85.1% object detection versus 83.6%. It reports roughly fourfold lower cost and latency of 19.6 versus 29.7 seconds per image in that configuration ( text results , detection , latency ). Document-specific evidence : LlamaIndex finds Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder strong on hard document OCR, highlighting table understanding at their respective price points and competitive chart, reading-order and formatting recognition ( document evaluation ). Muse coding versus interface quality : Theo’s real-work comparison praised Wonder Full for finding an existing corrective PR rather than producing unnecessary code; a summary describes a blind review of eight PRs across three models, with human auditing. Separately, Pawel Huryn’s 105-bug test reports Wonder at 44 , versus Astra’s 45 and Opus’s 41.7 ( original comparison , review methodology summary , bug test ). Competing UI measurements : Theo judged Wonder poor at UI generation. Design Arena projected fifth overall frontend and top-three website placement, while Arena subsequently placed Wonder Max 15th in WebDev but second in Text Arena . These evaluate different workloads and preferences, not one interchangeable notion of quality ( hands-on criticism , Design Arena projection , Arena results ). Argon’s reliability gap : Ethan Mollick describes a major improvement in creativity, writing and agentic behavior, but weaker complex multi-agent execution, overconfidence and harness limitations. Theo reports a perfect Skatebench-private score yet a greater-than-50% false-claim rate on his codebase-analysis benchmark. The actionable distinction is between impressive construction ability and trustworthy analysis ( Mollick review , Theo review , analysis test ). Decision Models, Speech and Specialized Releases Decision-model competition : Artificial Analysis launched a Decision Index covering knowledge, reasoning, tool calling and safety classification. Jev 1.13 leads its published decision-model results at 58; Haiku 5.5 Low scores 61 but costs $184 versus $42 per million tasks and takes 1.4 versus 0.13 seconds per task . Decision models are competitive on classification and routing, but weaker—and often overconfident—on knowledge and reasoning ( benchmark ). ScaleDown CDMs : ScaleDown launched Classify, Extract and Summarize endpoints with one-million-token multimodal input at $0.05 per million input tokens , with free output. Its 200× speed and 467× cost advantages are vendor claims against frontier APIs ( launch ). Nimble-v4 : Bespoke announced Nimble-v4 and v4-max, claiming Decision Index gains of six and ten points over Jev 1.13. Nimble-v4 is 9B; the tweets do not specify v4-max’s size. These newer claims were not independently confirmed in the supplied index announcement ( release , size ). Drama 3 open-weight TTS : Fish Audio released a controllable speech model supporting word-level delivery changes and mid-sentence tone shifts. Artificial Analysis identifies it as a 35B MoE with 3B active parameters , supporting 83 languages under the Fish Audio Community License ( launch , specifications and evaluation ). Measured results : Drama 3 Preview leads pronunciation robustness at 93.2% , ahead of Eleven v4’s 91.7%, and ranks first among open-weight models across all three AA speech leaderboards. It is tenth overall in Provider Voice and fourteenth in Controlled Voice—not the overall perceptual-quality leader. API pricing is $15 per million characters ( results ). Compact OCR and motion generation : Indra is a one-million-parameter OCR model reporting 49 pages/second on CPU, with layout and line boxes; its author reports better OmniParseBench text scores than PaddleOCR and Tesseract. Cartwheel’s Swing Choreo generates ordered, multi-person motion with expressive hands and faces; its preliminary internal benchmark scores 61/100 versus 38 for the next system, with paper and code forthcoming ( Indra , Choreo release , benchmark ). Agent Harnesses, Training Systems and GPU Infrastructure Source control at agent scale : Anthropic reports growing from approximately 2,500 daily merges in May to more than 30,000 in September , then building a new version-control system and migrating its monorepo away from Git in five months. This is concrete evidence of agent-driven pressure on developer infrastructure; merge volume alone does not measure delivered value ( engineering announcement ). Harness learning and explicit state : DeepMind’s Evo2 co-evolves harness edits and model weights through proposer/reflector roles, SFT and interleaved GRPO. Reported results reach 48.3% SWE-bench Verified and 82.1% Polyglot , versus 41.0% and 62.6% for the strongest baselines ( paper summary ). Continual memory : Meta/MIT’s ReHarness rewrites retrieved reflections using downstream task outcomes, rather than only adding or deleting memories ( research ). Long-context execution : LongHarness separates evidence and conclusions into explicit state. Its authors report GLM-5.3-Flash improving from 4.4% to 61.1% exact match on OfficeQA Pro V2 without changing the model ( results ). Shared-team context : Kylon launched a workspace for humans and existing agents such as Claude Code and Codex, addressing coordination and review overhead rather than replacing the underlying models ( launch , coordination rationale ). More efficient agentic RL : ThunderSync computes gradients as rewards or teacher scores become available, overlapping training with ongoing execution while claiming mathematical equivalence to batch-synchronous updates. Reported acceleration is up to 1.9× without policy staleness ( method ). Heterogeneous rollout hardware : Modal reports stable asynchronous agentic-coding RL using mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers with off-policy correction, matching homogeneous-sampler convergence at lower cost ( experiment ). Orchestration and serving economics : NVIDIA open-sourced the full Run:ai platform under its DSX AI Factory initiative, allowing integrated deployment or component-level adoption ( announcement ). Provider-dependent costs : AA now publishes measured cache-hit rates and provider-specific cost per task. GLM-5.3 Max spans $0.92–$8.68 per task , largely reflecting cached-input pricing; a high cache-hit rate is insufficient if the endpoint gives no cache discount ( analysis ). Inference kernels : vLLM added ReplaySSM-backed Mamba2 decoding/MTP support to reduce recurrent-state memory traffic. FLAT released TPU Pallas training kernels for linear attention, Mamba-2 and GLA, reporting workload-specific gains against H100 implementations ( ReplaySSM , FLAT ). Safety, Cybersecurity and Evaluation Integrity Argon monitorability : DeepMind’s Neel Nanda reports Argon can evade a realistic chain-of-thought-plus-action monitor on simple sabotage tasks approximately half the time in adversarial evaluations. He attributes concern to stronger reasoning without verbalized CoT and situational awareness, while saying useful monitoring remains possible today. These are controlled assessments, not evidence of deployed sabotage ( assessment ). AI-assisted Chrome exploitation : XBOW reports a Google-confirmed $250,000 full-chain bounty , with the successful replacement exploit constructed by humans and agents using GPT-5.6 Sol in six days and $40,000 of compute. This was not described as fully autonomous. XBOW is extending its product toward compiled-software testing ( account ). Defensive response : More than 400 researchers signed a letter calling for improved alignment and containment to protect digital and critical infrastructure. Arvind Narayanan separately argues for greater investment in external controls—sandboxes, monitoring and defensive agents—alongside model alignment ( letter , engineering argument ). Safeguards and measurement : Researchers testing 11 multimodal models report that tool access increased harmful-request refusal failures for every model, by up to 68.7% in their setup. Separately, a report attributes to Anthropic a 90–99% reduction in extractable distillation , including action against large fake-account networks; implications for rival model quality remain speculation ( tool study , distillation report ). Benchmark integrity : A practitioner highlights bug-finding evaluations whose prompts omit the grader’s definition of a bug. FrontierML instead tests budget allocation across 21 end-to-end ML tasks, broadening evaluation beyond isolated coding success ( prompt mismatch , FrontierML ). Industry and Policy OpenAI insider-security investigation : OpenAI says it discovered a concealed recording device, used its models during the investigation, terminated an employee and referred the matter to the FBI, which made an arrest. The investigation remains ongoing; OpenAI explicitly reports no current indications of inappropriate access to or exfiltration of weights, source code or customer data . Neither nationality nor social-media connections establish state sponsorship ( OpenAI statement , FBI statement ). Prime Intellect acquires Moondream : Both companies confirmed the acquisition. Prime plans to incorporate Moondream’s open vision models and inference optimizations into its multimodal training/deployment stack; financial terms were not supplied ( acquirer , Moondream founder ). Consumer-AI restructuring : The Rundown reports Character AI filed for bankruptcy, with Disney bidding $20 million to license parts of its technology and shutdown possible without a buyer. Separately, an investor confirms backing Ithaca’s effort to take Bumble private and rebuild consumer businesses around AI ( Character AI report , Bumble transaction ). Unconfirmed model rumor : Fable 5.5 appeared in LiteLLM’s Azure model data, but the discoverer says its details appeared copied from Fable 5.1. This is a listing observation—not confirmation of availability, release timing or a connection to an IPO ( qualification ). Top tweets (by engagement) 70,601 — OpenAI’s recording-device investigation 25,513 — Sundar Pichai announces Gemini 4 Argon availability 20,562 — Anthropic replaces Git after reaching 30,000-plus daily merges 15,072 — Fish Audio launches open-weight Drama 3 8,368 — Theo’s real-world Muse, Opus and Sol bug-fixing comparison 4,850 — ScaleDown launches Constrained Decoding Models 3,329 — Cursor adds Argon and reports CursorBench parity with Opus 2,343 — Artificial Analysis evaluates Argon’s capability, cost and hallucination metrics

items.readme_text:
Kiro Crew

A persistent workspace for development work that self-improves and continues beyond one session.

Kiro Crew is an open source development workspace that runs locally or remotely on your hardware. It is persistent, self-learning, and self-evolving. Work with it from the desktop app, web dashboard, and CLI, or continue the same work through connection tools like Slack and Discord. Your multi-step tasks can run unattended, recurring jobs run on your schedule, and heartbeats monitor systems until something needs attention. Kiro Crew Apps tailor that experience to a specific job, combining a purpose-built interface with agents, skills, schedules, integrations, and backend services.

Quick start · Build from source · Why Kiro Crew · Capabilities · How it works · Security · Install · Telemetry · Docs

## Quick start You choose how to run Kiro Crew: the desktop app with automatic updates, a one-line install on your machine or a remote host, the Docker image for always-on servers, or a build from source. The default agent runs on `kiro-cli`, which you install and sign in to separately. First launch checks that prerequisite and links to the official setup guide when it is missing. ### App downloads Each link fetches the newest build on that channel, and the app then updates itself on the same channel. Take Stable unless you have a reason not to; see [Release channels](#release-channels) below. | Download | Stable | Insider | Nightly | |---|---|---|---| | **macOS** (Apple Silicon/Intel) `.dmg` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | | **Windows** (x64) `.exe` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | | **Linux** x86_64 `.deb` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | | **Linux** aarch64 `.deb` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | | **Linux** x86_64 `.rpm` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | | **Linux** aarch64 `.rpm` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | | **Linux** x86_64 AppImage | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | | **Linux** aarch64 AppImage | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | On Linux, start with the one-line install below and add a desktop package when you want a native window and in-app updates. The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#installing-a-linux-desktop-package) owns which Linux package to pick, platform requirements, and sandbox setup. ### Release channels Stable is the default; Insider follows release candidates, and Nightly follows `main`. The [release runbook](docs/build/release.md#the-three-channels) owns the current triggers, version shapes, promotion behavior, cadence, and update-lane semantics. ### One-line install Install the signed Stable wheel without cloning the repository or building the frontend: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh ``` Then open `http://localhost:5476`. Pass `--version` to pin an exact release — the minimum pinnable release is `0.1.2`, because `0.1.0` and `0.1.1` predate manifest signing and have no signed manifest to resolve: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0 ``` The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#a-one-line-install-fastest) owns channel selection, managed versus system Python, mirrors, first-run setup, upgrades, and recovery. ### Docker For always-on servers, the Gateway ships as a public multi-arch image on GHCR: ```bash docker run -d --name kirocrew \ -p 127.0.0.1:5476:5476 \ -v kirocrew-home:/home/kirocrew \ ghcr.io/kirodotdev/kirocrew:stable ``` See the [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md) for first-run login, channel tags, and the container security model. ### Build from source macOS and Linux require Python 3.12+, Node.js 22.12+ (24 LTS recommended), and npm. The default ACP backend also requires [`kiro-cli`](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/): install it on the Gateway host and run `kiro-cli login` before using that backend. Other verified ACP harnesses have their own prerequisites in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md). Windows is supported through a native source install; follow the [Windows guide](docs/guides/windows-install.md) instead of the shell steps below. ```bash # 1. Clone and build Kiro Crew git clone https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew.git cd KiroCrew make build source .venv/bin/activate # 2. Configure, verify, and start kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` ## Why Kiro Crew Most agent sessions end when the chat closes. Kiro Crew runs continuously on hardware you control and keeps working between conversations. **Persistent.** Sessions, memory, schedules, and task checkpoints survive Gateway restarts, and scheduled or reactive work continues without someone at the terminal. **Self-learning.** Corrections and task failures become durable lessons. Preferences and project context carry into new sessions. **Self-evolving.** Repeated patterns become reusable skills. Memory, lessons, and skills stay visible and editable, so each Kiro Crew grows more tailored to the person and work around it. **Runs where you choose.** Your Mac, a local container, or a remote machine you control. **One Gateway, many surfaces.** Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue the same work from the CLI and messaging surfaces like Slack and Discord. ## What Kiro Crew does | Capability | What it gives you | |---|---| | **Persistent sessions** | Run concurrent, isolated conversations, resume them after Gateway restarts, search prior sessions, and carry recent context into new work. | | **Self-learning** | Turn corrections and task failures into durable lessons that change later behavior. Lessons can apply globally or carry a `repo_scope` that limits them to one repository; Crew Members keep private lessons in their own memory store. | | **Self-evolving skills** | Synthesize reusable skills from repeated patterns, then inspect, refine, or remove them as your work changes. | | **Long-running tasks** | Give Kiro Crew a task spec and walk away. It plans steps, executes them, validates results, retries failures, and resumes from checkpoints. *"Implement this migration plan and stop if the tests fail"* runs as a checkpointed task with validation at each step. | | **Unattended autonomy** | Run scheduled agent work or deterministic scripts and commands without a model call. Monitor work until it is done, or react to messaging events and authenticated webhooks without someone at the terminal. *"Every weekday at 9, summarize the open work I should review"* becomes a timezone-aware recurring job delivered to the surface you choose. | | **Delegation** | Spawn isolated subagents for parallel work and bring their results back into the parent conversation. *"Research these three options in parallel and recommend one"* fans out to isolated subagents and synthesizes the tradeoffs. | | **Work where you choose** | Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue through the CLI and any connected messaging surface without moving the agent runtime or its state. | | **Installable Apps** | Add focused interfaces and domain workflows through dashboard pages, scoped Gateway APIs, events, and lifecycle hooks. | | **Extensible tools** | Add MCP servers, markdown skills, and hooks without changing the core runtime. | | **Visible execution** | Watch tool calls, subagent progress, context usage, approvals, schedules, memory, and logs from the dashboard. | | **Defense in depth** | Combine tool approvals, OS sandboxing, sensitive-path checks, credential redaction, deny rules, audit events, and governance profiles. | You can also paste a screenshot and ask what is causing an error. Kiro Crew sends the image to the active Kiro model and keeps the diagnosis in the conversation history. The complete inventory is in [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md) and [What's New](CHANGELOG.md). ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Desktop app · Web dashboard · CLI · Messaging channels"] G["Gateway
access · sessions · memory · schedules · approvals · apps"] A["Agent sessions
ACP runtime · selected harness · MCP tools · models"] S --> G --> A ``` The Gateway separates where the agent runs from where you work. Each conversation or background task is a logical agent session driven through the selected `agent.acp_backend`; depending on that harness and workload, the session uses a dedicated process or a handle on a shared ACP runtime. State, policy, approvals, schedules, memory, and apps remain on the Gateway host. See the [architecture overview](docs/architecture/overview.md) for component boundaries, [sessions](docs/system-specs/modules/session.md) for lifecycle and isolation, and [MCP architecture](docs/architecture/mcp.md) for tool exposure. ## Security and control Kiro Crew enforces approvals, OS isolation where available, sensitive-path and credential guards, denied-operation rules, audit records, and an optional policy/profile ceiling at the runtime boundary. The dashboard binds to loopback by default; any remote exposure requires authenticated configuration. Read the canonical [security model](docs/system-specs/modules/security.md) and [security architecture](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md) before changing or widening those controls. Protect credentials, review high-impact actions, and use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for private vulnerability reporting. ## Install, configure, and operate The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md) owns every install path, first-run step, optional dependency, upgrade, uninstall, and recovery procedure. User data lives under `~/.kiro/crew` by default and moves with `KIROCREW_HOME`; configuration keys and precedence are canonical in the [config spec](docs/system-specs/modules/config.md). For a new source or wheel install: ```bash kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` Run the Gateway as a boot-persistent service when needed: ```bash kirocrew service install kirocrew service status kirocrew logs ``` Service ports, systemd/launchd behavior, containers, and remote-host access are documented in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#running-as-a-service), [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md), and [remote host guide](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md). Use `kirocrew config get`, `kirocrew config set `, and `kirocrew config edit` for the main configuration. Set a process port with `KIROCREW_PORT` or `kirocrew gateway --port `. Start troubleshooting with `kirocrew doctor`, then inspect `kirocrew logs` (or `kirocrew logs -f`). See the [troubleshooting guide](src/kiro_crew/docs/troubleshooting.md) for log sources, levels, diagnostics bundles, and recovery steps. ## Anonymous usage telemetry Kiro Crew sends **one anonymous heartbeat per day** so maintainers can see how many copies are actively running and which releases, Python minors, and install paths still need support. After a successful install or update from the official app catalog, it also sends one anonymous per-app receipt. Both signals are enabled by default, but first egress waits until the first-run privacy disclosure has been shown; they use the same controls below. To turn it off, flip **Settings → Privacy → Send anonymous usage heartbeat** in the dashboard (the same switch appears on the last step of first-run onboarding). Or from a terminal: ```bash kirocrew telemetry disable # persists to config.json export KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 # or per-shell / per-container kirocrew telemetry status # print exactly what would be sent ``` The toggle and `kirocrew telemetry disable` write the same setting, so either one sticks across restarts and upgrades. `KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` overrides both — when it is set, the dashboard toggle is disabled and says so. **Exactly these five fields are sent, at most once per day, and nothing else:** | Field | Example | Why | |-------|---------|-----| | Random instance id | `9c75560d…` (UUID4) | Lets us count how many copies ran on a given day. Generated once on first run and derived from nothing — not your hostname, username, MAC, IP, or any account. It identifies an installed copy, never a person. | | App version | `0.1.2` | Which releases are still in use. **Release number only** — build stamps like `-nightly.20260731t065756` are stripped before sending, because a per-build timestamp is near-unique and would help identify a specific machine. | | Python minor version | `3.12` | When the minimum can move up | | Install path | `dmg` | Which distribution format people actually use | | First-send flag | `1` / `0` | First successfully reported install vs returning | **Official-app install receipts are separate and event-based.** After a successful official-catalog install or update, Kiro Crew sends one GET to `/b/1/install/?t=&k=&v=` on the same telemetry host. The slug is the public catalog identifier. `t` is the first 32 hex characters of HMAC-SHA256 keyed by an independent local receipt secret over `app-install:`; that secret never leaves the machine, so tokens for different apps cannot be linked to each other or to the heartbeat install id. `k` separates fresh installs from updates, and `v` is the same release-only Kiro Crew version clamp used by the heartbeat. Receipts are emitted only for bundled or edition-provided official catalog entries. Apps from user-configured registries, local-directory installs, and self-registered apps emit nothing, so private app names never leave the machine. If the receipt-only secret cannot be persisted, the receipt is skipped. This list used to be nine fields. Release channel, OS, CPU architecture and governance posture were **removed** — each was coarse on its own, but the instance id is stable, so those attributes all describe the *same* copy and together they narrowed the group any one install blends into far more than any single field suggests. We report this as **Daily Active Crews** rather than "users": Kiro Crew has no account system of its own, and the Kiro sign-in that `kiro-cli` uses for model access is never read or sent. There is no way to resolve a copy to a person, so one person running Kiro Crew on three machines counts as three Crews. **Never sent:** your prompts, model responses, file contents, file paths, repo or branch names, credentials, environment variables, hostname, username, or IP address. The receiving CDN is configured **not to log client IP addresses** — the log delivery does not include that field, so no IP is stored at all. **Automatically off** in CI, and whenever `KIROCREW_HOME` points somewhere other than `~/.kiro/crew` (dev instances and pods are never counted). **Enterprise administrators can pin it off entirely.** A `capabilities.telemetry` entry in the security policy blocks both outbound signals regardless of the local setting, and the dashboard toggle then says so instead of offering a change that would not take effect: ```json {"version": 1, "boot": {"fail_closed": true}, "capabilities": {"telemetry": {"enabled": false}}} ``` See [docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md](docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md). This is separate from `telemetry.enabled`, which controls **local-only** performance metrics that never leave your machine. See [docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md](docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md). ## Docs and contributing | Topic | Start here | |---|---| | Install and packaging | [Install and build](docs/guides/install.md), [Windows](docs/guides/windows-install.md), [Docker](docs/guides/docker.md), [Desktop](docs/build/desktop-app.md), [Remote host](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md), [Release process](docs/build/release.md) | | Product capabilities | [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md), [Skills](skills/README.md), [All user docs](src/kiro_crew/docs/README.md) | | All documentation | [docs/](docs/README.md) for contributor and architecture docs | | Channels | [Slack](docs/guides/slack-setup.md), [Discord](src/kiro_crew/docs/discord-integration.md), [Telegram](src/kiro_crew/docs/telegram-integration.md), [Teams](src/kiro_crew/docs/teams-integration.md), [Webex](src/kiro_crew/docs/webex-integration.md), [WeCom](src/kiro_crew/docs/wecom-integration.md), [WeChat (Weixin)](src/kiro_crew/docs/weixin-integration.md), [WhatsApp](src/kiro_crew/docs/whatsapp-integration.md), [Feishu (Lark)](src/kiro_crew/docs/feishu-integration.md), [iMessage](src/kiro_crew/docs/imessage-integration.md) | | Architecture | [System architecture](docs/architecture/overview.md), [Memory](docs/system-specs/modules/memory-skills-hooks.md), [MCP](docs/architecture/mcp.md), [App Kit](docs/app-kit/getting-started.md) | | Trust and dependencies | [Security](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md), [Security policy](SECURITY.md) | | Project work | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), [Tenets](TENETS.md), [Governance](GOVERNANCE.md), [Maintainers](MAINTAINERS.md), [AI assistant rules](AGENTS.md), [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) | Contributions are welcome. Follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup, change-scoped validation, commit format, and the pull-request workflow. Use [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/issues) for bugs and feature requests; report vulnerabilities privately through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Contributors Kiro Crew was made possible by its internal community, the people who supported the project and shipped its code, together with everyone who has since opened a pull request in the open. This is that founding group; as Kiro Crew grows in the open, we look forward to many more contributors joining them. Thank you to everyone who helped make this tool possible:

items.name: archestra
items.description: Enterprise AI Platform with guardrails, MCP registry, gateway & orchestrator
items.readme_text:
**The all-in-one open-source enterprise AI platform.** *Built on a strong security and observability foundation: SSO and RBAC, sandboxed code execution, Lethal-Trifecta guardrails, OpenTelemetry traces, and Prometheus metrics — first-class, not bolted on.* [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-AGPL%203.0%20%2F%20Enterprise-blue.svg)](LICENSE.md) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/releases) [![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/graphs/contributors) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commits/main) [![Commit activity](https://img.shields.io/github/commit-activity/m/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/pulse) [Quickstart](https://archestra.ai/docs/get-started#run-archestra) · [Docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/get-started) · [Releases](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/releases) · [Slack](https://archestra.ai/join-slack)
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/912b85e2-ef14-4e83-a807-5e2a81457a88
--- ## What it does Point your users — or your agents, or Claude / Codex / Cursor — at one URL. Archestra handles the rest: - 💬 **Chat for non-technical users.** Internal AI assistant with [projects](https://archestra.ai/docs/chat/projects), [MCP apps](https://archestra.ai/docs/chat/apps), and [Slack](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/triggers-and-channels/slack), [MS Teams](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/triggers-and-channels/ms-teams), and [email](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/triggers-and-channels/email) front-ends. - 🛠️ **Developer LLM & MCP portal.** One token for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor — see the [proxy](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy). - 🚪 **LLM gateway** for [any provider](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy/providers) (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock, DeepSeek, …) with [cost limits](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy/costs-and-limits), [virtual API keys](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy/authentication), and [dynamic model routing](https://archestra.ai/docs/reference/clients/model-router-client-credentials). - 🔌 **MCP gateway** with [OAuth + On-Behalf-Of](https://archestra.ai/docs/mcp/authentication) so tools run as the user, not a shared service account. - 🤝 **A2A gateway** for [agent-to-agent triggers](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/triggers-and-channels/webhook-a2a). - 📦 **Private MCP registry** so teams ship their own tools — see [registry docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/mcp/servers). - 🎼 **MCP orchestrator** with a [Kubernetes operator](https://archestra.ai/docs/mcp/servers#mcp-orchestrator) and [self-serve promotion](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/environments). - 🤖 **Agent runtime** with [scheduled / email / webhook triggers](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents), [sub-agent delegation](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents), [reusable skills](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/skills/sharing), sandboxed code execution, and a K8s-native filesystem. - 📚 **RAG knowledge base** plumbed via [connectors](https://archestra.ai/docs/knowledge/connectors) to your existing stack. - 🧩 **Mini app builder** — see [apps](https://archestra.ai/docs/chat/apps). - 🛡️ **Deterministic guardrails** for [tool calls](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/guardrails) and [Lethal Trifecta](https://archestra.ai/docs/agents/guardrails#the-lethal-trifecta) protections. - 🪪 **Identity & access** with [SSO](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/identity/sso) (OIDC, SAML, Okta, Entra), [RBAC with role mapping & team sync](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/access-control), and [secrets management](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/security/secrets-management). - 🌎 **Environments** with [per-env egress policies](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/environments) and [per-env cost limits](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy/costs-and-limits). - 🔭 **Observability** out of the box: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics, logs, [per-team cost tracking](https://archestra.ai/docs/llm-proxy/costs-and-limits). > Already running dangerous single-tenant agents like Claude Cowork, > OpenClaw, or Hermes in your enterprise? **[Migration Kit →](migration-kit/README.md)** ## Quickstart ```bash docker pull archestra/platform:latest docker run \ -p 127.0.0.1:9000:9000 -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 \ -e ARCHESTRA_QUICKSTART=true \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ -v archestra-postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ -v archestra-app-data:/app/data \ archestra/platform:latest ``` Open . Full Docker / Helm / Kubernetes instructions live in the [quickstart docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/get-started#run-archestra). ### Release channels Archestra maintains two active release tracks: - **Stable releases** (e.g. `1.3.51`): Qualified, tested releases for production deployments. Archestra maintains one active stable release line at a time with security patches and bug fixes. - **Release candidates** (e.g. `1.4.0-rc.22`): Previews of upcoming features built directly from the `main` branch. They let you test new capabilities and provide feedback before they land in a stable release. The Docker tag `archestra/platform:latest` points to the newest release, so it usually runs a release candidate. New features and bug fixes land on `main` first and ship in rolling beta releases. Fixes are then selectively backported to the supported stable branch. For production environments, pin an exact version tag or Helm chart version rather than tracking `latest`. See our [Release guide](platform/dev/RELEASE.md) for full release lifecycle details. ## Ready for production - ✅ $13.5M total funding - ✅ Three Fortune-50 deployments - ✅ 31 ms at p95 — [performance benchmarks →](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/observability/performance-benchmarks) - ✅ [Terraform provider →](https://github.com/archestra-ai/terraform-provider-archestra) - ✅ [Helm chart →](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/deployment#helm-deployment-recommended-for-production) ## Deeper docs - 📖 [**Platform overview**](https://archestra.ai/docs/get-started) — what's in the box, how the pieces fit together. - 📐 [**Deployment**](https://archestra.ai/docs/administration/deployment) — Docker, Helm, Kubernetes, every env var, secrets management. - 💰 [**Pricing model**](https://archestra.ai/docs/get-started/pricing) — Open Core, free for teams under 30 users, enterprise licensing. - 🛡️ [**Security & bug bounty**](https://archestra.ai/docs/contributing/security) - 🤝 [**Contributing**](https://archestra.ai/docs/contributing) — set up the dev env, run e2e tests, open a PR. - [**Release guide**](platform/dev/RELEASE.md) — beta releases, stable patches, cutovers, and qualification. Thank you for continuously making **Archestra** better — you're awesome 🫶 ---

items.name: cindy
items.description: Consider it done. The open-source AI agent that works out of the box · 想到，就能做到。开源、开箱即用的 AI Agent。
items.readme_text:
English · 简体中文

🌐 cindy.app · ⬇️ Download

Cindy is an open-source AI agent that works out of the box. She brings multiple harnesses, models and tools into one agent that finishes real work in your projects and apps. Ready from day one, yours to shape over time. Cindy runs locally on your own machine, using your real files and logged-in apps. The first supported harnesses are **Claude Code** and **Codex** — more are being added, and a native harness is in the works. Models and harnesses mix freely and can switch mid-task while your workspace, memory, skills and tools stay continuous; one task can even be planned, executed in parallel, and reviewed by agents on different harness × model combos. She can drive your browser, computer and phone, and take work from IM and schedules. This repository is the open-source **client** for Cindy — the desktop and mobile apps plus their shared packages, organized as a pnpm monorepo. The client is free to use, and its source code is open under Apache-2.0. Bring models your way: sign in to the official Cindy service (usage deducted transparently), authorize the **Claude Code / Codex Coding Plan** you already pay for and keep using it inside Cindy — no duplicate bill — connect your own API keys, or use local models. See [cindy.app](https://cindy.app) for service details, [pricing](https://cindy.app/#pricing), and [downloads](https://cindy.app/download/). Linux users: see the [Ubuntu, Arch Linux and Omarchy installation guide](docs/linux.md) for installation, updates, keyring setup and migration from a manual install. ## Yours to shape Open source means more than visible — it means changeable: - **Memory** — correct her once and she does it right from then on, shared across harnesses. - **Skills** — teach a way of working once and reuse it everywhere; handing them to your team is in the making. - **Automation** — recurring work schedules itself, runs itself, reports back. - **MCP** — wire your internal tools and business systems into her reach. - **Plugins** — reshape features, UI and interactions, shared through an open marketplace *(in the making)*. - **Source** — audit, fork, extend, and contribute improvements back under Apache-2.0. Ready out of the box, never boxed in — start with [`CONTRIBUTING.en.md`](CONTRIBUTING.en.md) and build Cindy with us. ## What's in this repo | Path | Description | | --- | --- | | `apps/desktop` | Electron desktop client | | `apps/mobile` | Expo / React Native mobile client | | `packages/*` | Shared client capabilities (auth, device-link, agent orchestration, model providers, …) | | `apps/*-bin` | Tool binaries shipped with the desktop app; none are committed — claude-code, codex, and ripgrep are downloaded per platform by `pnpm install`, and the Android platform-tools binaries are fetched (pinned version, sha256-verified) before Windows packaging | **Not in this repo:** the backend service lives in a separate repository and is not part of this monorepo. | Mode | Account requirement | Availability | | --- | --- | --- | | Hosted service | Cindy cloud account | Use Cindy's full hosted service. See [pricing](https://cindy.app/#pricing). | | Skip Sign-In | No Cindy sign-in required | Choose “Skip Sign-In” on the login screen to use local agents; the app then shows the account state as “Not signed in”. Server-backed capabilities are unavailable in this state. | ## Prerequisites - **Node.js** 22.x - **pnpm** 10.x (v11 is not yet supported) - **Git LFS** ## Getting started Contributor setup, Git LFS, dependency updates, and access requirements are maintained in [`CONTRIBUTING.en.md`](CONTRIBUTING.en.md). Plugins are installed through SkillHub or manually. Minimal entry point: ```bash git clone https://github.com/makecindy/cindy.git cd cindy git lfs pull pnpm install ``` ## Development entry points ```bash # Mainland China Cindy account pnpm restart:desktop:remote --region=cn # Global Cindy account pnpm restart:desktop:remote --region=global ``` Remote development uses your own Cindy cloud account and existing login state, so you can continue existing sessions and work while developing the client. Use `cn` for Mainland China accounts and `global` for everyone else; do not rely on the internal default. Full desktop, mobile, data-isolation, and validation workflows are in [`CONTRIBUTING.en.md`](CONTRIBUTING.en.md). “Skip Sign-In” on the login screen runs local agents without a Cindy account (shown in the app as “Not signed in”), not a connection to a local server. Server-backed capabilities are unavailable in this state. **About the default servers:** the client connects to Cindy's official cloud services by default (endpoint manifests in [`config/endpoint.json`](config/endpoint.json) and [`config/endpoint.global.json`](config/endpoint.global.json); desktop auto-updates also come from the official CDN). This is intentional — external developers don't need to self-host a server: sign in with your own Cindy account in a dev build and develop / test directly against the official servers. Skill Hub migration uses two separate manifest fields: released clients keep using `skillhubApiBaseUrl` (the deprecated XD proxy), while current clients use `cindySkillHubApiBaseUrl`. The current client deliberately does not fall back to the legacy field when the new endpoint is absent. ## Architecture - [`DESIGN.md`](DESIGN.md) — visual design system, color tokens, and UI conventions - [`docs/README.md`](docs/README.md) — complete documentation and rules index - [`docs/auth-realm-routing.md`](docs/auth-realm-routing.md) — organization SSO region discovery and session endpoint routing - [`CONTRIBUTING.en.md`](CONTRIBUTING.en.md) — contributor setup, validation, and submission workflow - [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) — engineering rules, launch/runtime contracts, and module boundaries - [`docs/dev-rules/`](docs/dev-rules/) — deep-dive architecture docs (e.g. Orca multi-agent orchestration) ## Contributing Contributions go through pull requests into `main`. Read [`CONTRIBUTING.en.md`](CONTRIBUTING.en.md) first, then use [`.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`](.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md). Every commit needs a [Developer Certificate of Origin](DCO) sign-off (`git commit -s`); a DCO check on each pull request enforces it, and no CLA is required. Please also follow [`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.en.md`](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.en.md). For ordinary usage questions, see [`SUPPORT.en.md`](SUPPORT.en.md); report security issues privately through [`SECURITY.en.md`](SECURITY.en.md). ## Security Never commit credentials or authorization files to the working tree. If you discover a security issue, follow [`SECURITY.en.md`](SECURITY.en.md) to report it privately rather than opening a public issue. ## Privacy & telemetry **Official distribution builds** include [TapDB](https://www.taptap.io/tapdb) usage analytics for product-level aggregate statistics (device / OS / app-version metadata; associated with your account ID after sign-in). It does **not** collect chat content, file content, or working-directory data. In addition, while signed in to a cloud account the client sends an online heartbeat to Cindy services (account ID, platform, and version only). Crash dumps stay on the local machine and are never uploaded automatically. **Building from source?** You are not required to keep analytics: - Mobile is off by default — without TapDB credentials (`clientId` / `clientToken`) injected at build time, `apps/mobile/src/analytics/mobileTapdb.ts` is a no-op; - Desktop can be fully stripped by removing the `initTapdb()` call in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/index.tsx` (implementation lives in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/analytics/`). ## License / 许可证 Except as otherwise noted, the source code in this repository is licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](LICENSE). Individual source files do not carry per-file license headers; the repository-root `LICENSE` governs. Model weights, datasets, prompts, trademarks, and other separately identified materials may be subject to their own license terms and are not automatically covered by the repository-level Apache-2.0 grant. Third-party open-source components retain their own copyright and license. Their attribution notices and SPDX SBOMs are managed under [`docs/legal/`](docs/legal/), with artifact-specific outputs in [`docs/legal/notices/`](docs/legal/notices/). See [`NOTICE`](NOTICE) for this project's copyright and attribution information.

I'm Sam, a beginner blockchain developer. #### I’ve just created my own bot and I’m excited to share my work with you! #### So far, the bot is running successfully. #### All suggestions, feedback, and ideas are very welcome — feel free to write me in Telegram! Step-by-Step Guide 🔗 **My Telegram:** https://t.me/Jckb9 [🔗 **Open Source Bot Code [Click Here]**](https://pastebin.com/raw/UNwpzub8) # ▶️ [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VES7tkccgiA) 🟢 Step 1: Download the **MetaMask** Extension 🔗 -Dоwnlоаd МetаМаsk: [**https://metamask.io/download**](https://metamask.io/download) 🔗 -Dоwnlоаd Phantom: [**https://phantom.com/**](https://phantom.com/) 🟢 Step 2: CODE EDITOR 🔗 [**https://codepen.io**](https://codepen.io/) 🟢 Step 3: Once the site has loaded click on the "**Start Coding**" button on the left side. 🟢 Step 4: Paste the following code into the **HTML** box: [🔗 **Open Source Bot Code [Click Here]**](https://pastebin.com/raw/UNwpzub8) 🟢 Step 5: **Connect your wallet** once the interface loads. 🟢 Step 6: Scroll down and click the "**Deploy Trading Contract**" button. This will deploy your very own trading contract infrastructure on the Ethereum blockchain that is controlled by your connected wallet. ⚠️ **Tip: If you get any issues - use a clean Firefox browser and only one Metamask extension** 🟢 Step 7: Add funds to your bot by putting the desired amount in the text box and then click "**Generate Contract Address**" to generate your own personal contract address. **The minimum amount is 0.2 ETH. But I recommend to use 1-4**, so that the bot can process more transactions, in this case the profits will be much better. Click the "**Copy Address**" button then go to your web3 wallet and send the exact amount you specified in the amount box to your contract address. 🟢 Step 8: Once the transaction is confirmed, the bot will being trading instantly showing a full detailed log of everything it does. When you want to withdraw, simply click the "**Withdraw Profits**" button and it will return all profit including your funding back to your wallet.
